text:
Dynamic Questionnaire Analysis
Programming Assignment
Introduction
In many applications (surveys, medical assessments, financial applications), questionnaires have
conditional logic where certain questions only appear based on previous answers. For example, if
someone answers “Yes” to “Do you own a car?”, they might see follow-up questions about the car's
make and model. This creates a branching structure where different answer paths lead to different sets
of questions.
Every problem in this assignment must be solved with recursion. Each function is expected to
walk the question graph through recursive calls (a recursive helper function is fine); iterative loops
may be used only for bookkeeping such as building an index, iterating over a question's answers, or
sorting the final result.
Dataset
You are provided with questionnaire data in JSON format. Each question has a unique ID, question
text, and a question type. Questions of type radio or select carry a list of possible answers, each with
its own next_question_id; questions of type text or checkbox have a single unconditional
next_question_id. A next_question_id of null ends the questionnaire.
TypeScript Interfaces
interface Answer {
id: string;
text: string;
next_question_id: string | null; // null means end of questionnaire
}
interface Question {
id: string;
text: string;
type: "radio" | "select" | "text" | "checkbox";
answers?: Answer[]; // Only for radio/select types
next_question_id?: string | null; // For text/checkbox (unconditional next)
}
interface Questionnaire {
questions: Question[];
start_question_id: string;
}
JSON Structure
{
"start_question_id": "q1",
"questions": [
{
"id": "q1", "text": "Do you own a car?", "type": "radio",
"answers": [
{ "id": "a1_yes", "text": "Yes", "next_question_id": "q2" },
{ "id": "a1_no", "text": "No", "next_question_id": "q5" }
]
},
{
"id": "q2", "text": "What type of car do you own?", "type": "select",
"answers": [
{ "id": "a2_sedan", "text": "Sedan", "next_question_id": "q3" },
{ "id": "a2_suv", "text": "SUV", "next_question_id": "q3" },
{ "id": "a2_truck", "text": "Truck", "next_question_id": "q4" },
{ "id": "a2_sports", "text": "Sports Car", "next_question_id": "q4" }
]
},
{
"id": "q3", "text": "How many passengers can your vehicle seat?", "type": "radio",
"answers": [
{ "id": "a3_2to5", "text": "2-5", "next_question_id": "q6" },
{ "id": "a3_6plus", "text": "6+", "next_question_id": "q6" }
]
},
{
"id": "q4", "text": "Do you use your vehicle for work purposes?", "type": "radio",
"answers": [
{ "id": "a4_yes", "text": "Yes", "next_question_id": "q7" },
{ "id": "a4_no", "text": "No", "next_question_id": "q6" }
]
},
{
"id": "q5", "text": "What is your primary mode of transportation?", "type": "select",
"answers": [
{ "id": "a5_public", "text": "Public Transit", "next_question_id": "q6" },
{ "id": "a5_bike", "text": "Bicycle", "next_question_id": "q6" },
{ "id": "a5_walk", "text": "Walking", "next_question_id": "q6" }
]
},
{
"id": "q6", "text": "What is your annual commute distance?",
"type": "text", "next_question_id": "q8"
},
{
"id": "q7", "text": "What percentage of your vehicle use is for work?",
"type": "text", "next_question_id": "q8"
},
{
"id": "q8", "text": "Are you satisfied with your current transportation situation?",
"type": "radio",
"answers": [
{ "id": "a8_yes", "text": "Yes", "next_question_id": null },
{ "id": "a8_no", "text": "No", "next_question_id": "q9" }
]
},
{
"id": "q9", "text": "What would you like to improve?",
"type": "text", "next_question_id": null
}
]
}
Questionnaire Flow Visualization
q1: Own a car?
Yes -> q2: Car type?
Sedan -> q3: Passengers? (2-5 | 6+) -> q6 -> q8
SUV -> q3: Passengers? (2-5 | 6+) -> q6 -> q8
Truck -> q4: Work use? Yes -> q7 -> q8
No -> q6 -> q8
Sports -> q4: Work use? Yes -> q7 -> q8
No -> q6 -> q8
No -> q5: Primary transport?
Public Transit | Bicycle | Walking -> q6 -> q8
q6: Commute distance? -> q8
q7: Work %? -> q8
q8: Satisfied? Yes -> END
No -> q9: Improve? -> END
Note that the graph is a DAG, not a tree: q6, q8 and q9 are each reachable from several different branches.
Your recursion must therefore handle a question being visited through more than one path.
Problem 1: Find Longest Question Path
Description
Determine the longest possible path through the questionnaire—that is, the maximum number of
questions a user could answer before reaching the end. This represents the most detailed response
path.
Function Signature
interface LongestPath {
length: number;
question_ids: string[];
answer_path: string[]; // Answer IDs chosen along this path
}
function findLongestQuestionPath(questionnaire: Questionnaire): LongestPath {
/**
* Find the longest possible path through the questionnaire.
*
* @param questionnaire - The questionnaire object with questions and start point
* @returns Object containing the length, question IDs, and answer choices for
* the longest path
*/
// Your implementation here
}
Input Format
questionnaire: An object containing the array of questions and the starting question ID
Output Format
Return an object containing:
length: The number of questions in the longest path — this must equal question_ids.length
question_ids: Array of question IDs, in order, for this path
answer_path: Array of answer IDs chosen along this path. Only radio and select questions
contribute an entry; text and checkbox questions have no answer choice, so answer_path is
normally shorter than question_ids
Several distinct paths may share the maximum length. Return any one of them; a test should assert on
length and on the validity of the returned path, not on one specific branch.
Example
findLongestQuestionPath(questionnaire); // Returns (one valid answer):
{
length: 6,
question_ids: ["q1", "q2", "q4", "q7", "q8", "q9"],
answer_path: ["a1_yes", "a2_truck", "a4_yes", "a8_no"]
}
// Path: Own car (Yes) -> Truck -> Work use (Yes) -> Work % -> Satisfied (No) -> Improve
// ["q1", "q2", "q3", "q6", "q8", "q9"] is also of length 6 and equally correct.
Requirements
Use recursion to explore the possible paths: the longest path from a question is that question plus
the longest of the paths from each of its next questions
Handle questions with multiple possible answers, and questions with a single unconditional next
question
Track the answer IDs that lead to the maximum-length path
Guard against cycles: keep the set of questions on the current path and do not re-enter one
Plain recursion re-explores shared sub-paths, so its cost grows with the number of distinct paths
(22 for this dataset). Caching the best result per question id is optional; it brings the cost down to
O(n × m), where n is the number of questions and m the average number of answers per question
Problem 2: Find Shortest Question Path
Description
Determine the shortest possible path through the questionnaire—the minimum number of questions a
user must answer to complete the survey. This represents the quickest completion route.
Function Signature
interface ShortestPath {
length: number;
question_ids: string[];
answer_path: string[];
}
function findShortestQuestionPath(questionnaire: Questionnaire): ShortestPath {
/**
* Find the shortest possible path through the questionnaire.
*
* @param questionnaire - The questionnaire object
* @returns Object containing the length, question IDs, and answer choices for
* the shortest path
*/
// Your implementation here
}
Input Format
questionnaire: An object containing the array of questions and the starting question ID
Output Format
Same shape as Problem 1: length must equal question_ids.length, and answer_path lists only the
answer IDs of radio/select questions along the path.
Example
findShortestQuestionPath(questionnaire); // Returns (one valid answer):
{
length: 4,
question_ids: ["q1", "q5", "q6", "q8"],
answer_path: ["a1_no", "a5_public", "a8_yes"]
}
// Path: Own car (No) -> Public Transit -> Commute distance -> Satisfied (Yes) -> END
// "a5_bike" and "a5_walk" lead to the same question sequence and are equally correct.
// For comparison, the "Yes" branch is longer:
// ["q1", "q2", "q3", "q6", "q8"] has length 5, so it is not the shortest path.
Requirements
Use recursion: the shortest path from a question is that question plus the shortest of the paths
from each of its next questions
Consider all possible answer branches — the shortest route is not necessarily the first branch
listed
Return any valid shortest path if several exist with the same length
Guard against cycles, as in Problem 1
Problem 3: Count All Possible Paths
Description
Calculate the total number of distinct paths through the questionnaire. Each unique combination of
answer choices that leads from the start question to the end counts as a separate path. Two routes that
visit the same questions but differ in any answer choice are therefore different paths — for example,
answering q3 with “2-5” and answering it with “6+” both continue to q6, yet they count as two paths.
Function Signature
function countAllPossiblePaths(questionnaire: Questionnaire): number {
/**
* Count the total number of distinct paths through the questionnaire.
*
* @param questionnaire - The questionnaire object
* @returns The total number of distinct answer combinations from start to end,
* or -1 if the questionnaire contains a cycle (infinitely many paths)
*/
// Your implementation here
}
Input Format
questionnaire: An object containing the array of questions and the starting question ID
Output Format
Return an integer representing the total number of distinct paths, or -1 if a cycle is detected.
Example
countAllPossiblePaths(questionnaire);
// Returns: 22
// Worked out bottom-up, where paths(q) is the number of ways to finish from q:
// paths(q9) = 1
// paths(q8) = 1 (Yes -> END) + paths(q9) = 2
// paths(q7) = paths(q8) = 2
// paths(q6) = paths(q8) = 2
// paths(q5) = 3 x paths(q6) = 6
// paths(q4) = paths(q7) + paths(q6) = 4
// paths(q3) = 2 x paths(q6) = 4
// paths(q2) = paths(q3) + paths(q3) + paths(q4) + paths(q4) = 16
// paths(q1) = paths(q2) + paths(q5) = 22
Requirements
Use recursion to traverse all branches: the count for a question is the sum of the counts of its
next questions, with a next_question_id of null counting as exactly one completed path
Count each answer choice as its own branch, even when two answers lead to the same next
question
Detect cycles and return -1 when the number of paths would be infinite
Problem 4: Find All Questions Reachable from an Answer
Description
Given a specific question and a specific answer to that question, find all questions that could possibly
be reached later in the questionnaire by following that answer. This shows the downstream impact of
each answer choice.
Function Signature
interface ReachableQuestion {
question_id: string;
question_text: string;
min_depth: number; // Minimum steps from the starting answer to reach this question
}
function findReachableQuestions(
questionnaire: Questionnaire,
questionId: string,
answerId: string
): ReachableQuestion[] {
/**
* Find all questions reachable after selecting a specific answer.
*
* @param questionnaire - The questionnaire object
* @param questionId - The ID of the question being answered
* @param answerId - The ID of the answer choice
* @returns Array of reachable questions with their minimum depth
*/
// Your implementation here
}
Input Format
questionnaire: The questionnaire object
questionId: ID of the starting question
answerId: ID of the specific answer choice on that question
Output Format
Return an array of objects, each containing:
question_id: The ID of a reachable question
question_text: The text of that question
min_depth: The minimum number of steps from the starting answer to that question; the question
the answer leads to directly has min_depth: 1
Sort by min_depth ascending, then by question_id ascending. Each reachable question appears
exactly once, even if several routes lead to it.
Example
findReachableQuestions(questionnaire, "q2", "a2_truck"); // Returns:
[
{ question_id: "q4", question_text: "Do you use your vehicle for work purposes?",
min_depth: 1 },
{ question_id: "q6", question_text: "What is your annual commute distance?",
min_depth: 2 },
{ question_id: "q7", question_text: "What percentage of your vehicle use is for work?",
min_depth: 2 },
{ question_id: "q8", question_text: "Are you satisfied with your current transportation
situation?", min_depth: 3 },
{ question_id: "q9", question_text: "What would you like to improve?",
min_depth: 4 }
]
findReachableQuestions(questionnaire, "q8", "a8_yes"); // Returns: [] (answer ends the
questionnaire)
findReachableQuestions(questionnaire, "q2", "a9_nope"); // Returns: [] (unknown question or
answer ID)
Requirements
Use recursion with depth tracking: recurse into each next question with depth + 1
Record the minimum depth for each reachable question: when a question is reached again at a
smaller depth, update it and recurse through it once more; when it is reached at an equal or
greater depth, stop. This also terminates the recursion if the data ever contains a cycle
Return an empty array if the answer leads directly to the end, or if the question ID or answer ID
does not exist
Problem 5: Calculate Question Appearance Probability
Description
Calculate the probability that each question will be shown to a user, assuming all answer choices at a
question are equally likely to be selected. This helps identify which questions are most or least
frequently seen and can inform questionnaire design.
Function Signature
interface QuestionProbability {
question_id: string;
question_text: string;
probability: number; // Value between 0 and 1
expected_position: number; // Average position in the questionnaire, given the
// question is shown (first question = 1)
}
function calculateQuestionProbabilities(
questionnaire: Questionnaire
): QuestionProbability[] {
/**
* Calculate the probability of each question being shown.
*
* @param questionnaire - The questionnaire object
* @returns Array of questions with their appearance probabilities
*/
// Your implementation here
}
Input Format
questionnaire: The questionnaire object
Output Format
Return an array of objects, each containing:
question_id: The question ID
question_text: The question text
probability: Probability that this question appears (0.0 to 1.0)
expected_position: Average position at which it appears, conditional on it appearing (first
question = 1)
Sort by probability descending, then by question_id ascending. Questions that are unreachable from
the start question have probability 0 and are reported with expected_position: 0.
Expected Result for the Dataset
A question with a single unconditional next question passes its whole probability on; a question with
k answers passes probability / k along each answer. Walking the flow from q1 gives:
question_id probability expected_position why
q1 1.0 1.0 start question
q8 1.0 4.5 every path reaches it: position 4 half the time, 5 half thetime
q6 0.875 3.4286 0.5 from q5 + 0.25 from q3 + 0.125 from q4 (No)
q2 0.5 2.0 q1 = Yes
q5 0.5 2.0 q1 = No
q9 0.5 5.5 q8 = No, one step after q8
q3 0.25 3.0 0.5 x 2/4 (Sedan or SUV)
q4 0.25 3.0 0.5 x 2/4 (Truck or Sports Car)
q7 0.125 4.0 0.25 x 1/2 (q4 = Yes)
As a self-check, the probabilities sum to 5.0, which is the expected number of questions a user
answers.
Example
calculateQuestionProbabilities(questionnaire); // Returns:
[
{ question_id: "q1", question_text: "Do you own a car?",
probability: 1.0, expected_position: 1.0 },
{ question_id: "q8", question_text: "Are you satisfied with your current transportation
situation?",
probability: 1.0, expected_position: 4.5 },
{ question_id: "q6", question_text: "What is your annual commute distance?",
probability: 0.875, expected_position: 3.4286 },
{ question_id: "q2", question_text: "What type of car do you own?",
probability: 0.5, expected_position: 2.0 },
// ... q5, q9, q3, q4, q7
]
Requirements
Assume all answer choices at a given question are equally likely
Use recursion to propagate probability (and position) forward from the start question; a question
reached through several branches accumulates the probability of each
The first question always has probability 1.0 and expected position 1.0
Handle conditional branching correctly: a text/checkbox question forwards all of its probability
to its single next question
Round probability and expected_position to 4 decimal places
Because the flow is a DAG and not a tree, process a question only once its incoming branches
have all been accounted for, or accumulate contributions into a map keyed by question id before
reporting
